items.text: COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO PROCUREMENT AND CONTRACTS

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the state finance law and the tax law, in relation to
implementing "The New York State Low Embodied Carbon Concrete Leadership Act"
items.lawCode: Amd §165, St Fin L; amd §606 Tax L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S542

SPONSOR: KAMINSKY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the state finance law and the tax law, in relation to
implementing "The New York State Low Embodied Carbon Concrete Leadership
Act"

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To establish a low embodied carbon procurement standard for concrete
used in public construction projects that will rapidly incentivize emis-
sions reductions throughout the concrete production process. The low
embodied carbon procurement standard will leverage the State's substan-
tial concrete purchasing power to catalyze low carbon alternative meth-
ods and products in the concrete and cement industries as a whole. The
standard would also establish New York as a leader in the emerging low
embodied carbon concrete sector, resulting in new economic activity and
job creation.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 defines terms and explanations for a number of elements impor-
tant to the understanding of deploying carbon capture technology in
concrete production.

Section 2b requires that facilities, transportation authorities and
institutions of the state, solicitation specifications of the office of
general services and any other agency, department, office, board or
commission mandate provisions including the incorporation of low
embodied carbon emissions selection standards that are governed by the
Global Warming Potential (GWP) quantified through certified Environ-
mental Product Declaration (EPD) for each concrete mix proposed in bids
by offerers. For the purposes of bid assessment, scoring and selection,
a price discount will be applied to bids that are certified to have the
lowest GWP values. The maximum discount to be applied for the lowest GWP
bids will not exceed 5%.

Section 2c describes the application of supplemental price discounts for
bids that incorporate a low carbon concrete breakthrough as defined in
this act. The low carbon concrete breakthrough supplemental price
discount reflects the necessity for innovation in concrete products and
processes to fully decarbonize concrete and cement production by the
year 2050, given the inherent and substantial carbon intensity of
aspects of cement production that cannot be entirely mitigated through
technologies, methods, and products that are widely established in the
marketplace and in construction practice today.

Section 2d stipulates that the State will establish criteria for certi-
fying low carbon concrete breakthrough technologies, methods, and
products that are eligible for the low carbon concrete breakthrough
supplemental price discount. Furthermore, the state shall establish
rules and guidelines whereby specific price discount rates for bids
certified to use low carbon breakthrough technologies, methods and
products shall be determined and applied to bids based on GWP perform-
ance.


Section 2e stipulates that bid opportunities that include multiple
concrete mixes will aggregate the GWP into a single score that will
serve as the basis of comparison. Additionally, the concrete products
must meet or exceed all

Section 2f stipulates that the low carbon procurement standard rules
defined in Section 2b and 2c shall be complied with by private firms
contracted by the State to complete State-funded construction projects
that involve the utilization of concrete.

Section 2g states that the commissioner will issue, publicize and
disseminate regulations for implementation and guidelines for the evalu-
ation of contracts, and provide for monitoring of implementation.

Section 2h stipulates that the Commissioner will submit a report annual-
ly to the legislature analyzing the costs and benefits of the low
embodied carbon concrete procurement standard pertaining to fiscal
impact and the State's carbon reduction goals. The Commissioner will
also recommend any additional incentives or requirements that may be
necessary to help the state meet its emissions reduction goals of the
2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA).

Section 3 amends section 606 of the tax law to establish a tax credit to
compensate for the costs incurred by concrete and concrete component
manufacturers to undertake Environmental Product Declaration (analysis)
at their manufacturing plants.

Section 3a defines terms and explanations for elements important to the
understanding of the EPD tax credit.

Section 3b states which types of commercial entities are eligible to
avail the EPD tax credit.

Section 3c states that i) the maximum tax credit amount that shall be
availed by commercial entities is the lessor of the full cost of EPD
analysis or $3,000; ii) the maximum number of plants that a single
commercial entity may be permitted to avail the tax credit for during a
given tax year is eight; and iii) that the tax credit may be availed for
EPD analysis procured during tax year 2021 and tax year 2022.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

More than 10 billion tons of concrete are produced globally each year,
making it the second-most used substance on earth after water. The
production of concrete's core ingredient cement accounts for up to 8% of
total global emissions. To bring the concrete and cement sectors in line
with the targets agreed upon in the Paris Agreement, annual emissions
must. fall by 16% by 2030. However, current trajectories project that
demand for both materials could increase by as much as 23% by 2050.Under
this business as usual scenario, production escalation on this scale
will release extraordinary levels of CO2 during the next three pivotal
decades.

Therefore reducing the embodied carbon of concrete - a measure of emis-
sions generated during the production process of materials before they
are utilized - is a critical front in the collective global effort to
preserve the climate. At the same time, concrete's unique potential to
permanently store and mineralize carbon must be unlocked and advanced
through both private and public sector commitments.  Indeed, deep
reductions in cement-based emissions paired with technological inno-
vations that maximize concrete's carbon storage potential could ulti-
mately result in carbon negativity to an outcome in which less carbon is
emitted in concrete production than is permanently secured in its utili-
zation or storage. Given the present-day volume of concrete utilized
annually and the rate of growth projected over the coming decades,
transforming concrete from a net carbon source to a net carbon sink
would have highly meaningful and quantifiable implications for the
climate.

The New York State Low Embodied Carbon Concrete Leadership Act proposes
a new procurement standard for public construction projects that would
place our state firmly in a leading position to bring about this transi-
tion. And this is a role that New York is exceptionally well positioned
to assume given the bold commitments established by the Climate Leader-
ship and Community Production Act of 2019, and the size and dynamism of
the state's economy and construction industries.

Indeed, the proposed bill would help advance the ambitious goals and
principles of the CLCPA, while expanding its reach to encompass a major
source of emissions currently left unaddressed. As a major purchaser of
concrete, a procurement standard of this kind would provide a powerful
market signal to concrete and cement manufacturers to pursue emissions
reductions throughout the concrete supply chain.  Further, because many
well-established emissions reduction measures that would be incentivized
by this policy are made at the manufacturing plant level, the State's
actions would have an immediate influence over the emissions profile of
concrete and cement supplied to the private sector at large.

The legislation's objectives align with the CLCPA's broad emissions
reduction targets, but also specifically with provisions related to the
15% of emissions reductions that will be achieved either through offsets
or by carbon dioxide removal (CDR) from the atmosphere.  Enhancing
concrete's capacity to utilize and permanently mineralize high levels of
carbon in its mass is the goal of several cutting-edge research initi-
atives and startup firms today, but in the future could represent a
scalable and standard feature of this incredibly common commodity. As a
promising medium for carbon storage, concrete would create a sink for
carbon sourced from capture and storage technologies at difficult to
decarbonize industrial facilities (such as cement), as well emerging
carbon removal technologies such as Direct Air Capture (DAC). The legis-
lation's competitive mechanism will continuously drive innovation in
this direction and includes a special provision that incentivizes the
adoption and utilization of carbon capture, utilization and/or storage
technology (CCUS).

While establishing the carbon emissions of concrete as a definitive
factor in the bid decision making process, the legislation would also
cap allowable price premiums for low embodied concrete, thus limiting
fiscal impact on the State of New York and its taxpayers.

Finally, to further incentivize participation by concrete manufacturers,
the legislation introduces a time limited tax credit for eligible local
firms. The credit would offset financial burdens incurred by manufactur-
ers in completing Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) analyses,
which are required for quantifying the embodied carbon emissions of
concrete products. Given that 1. the tax credit is scheduled to expire
in four years following program initiation; 2. EPD analyses are competi-
tively priced ($2,000 - $4,000 per plant on average); and 3. The limited
number of concrete manufacturing companies operating in the state, the
fiscal impact of the credit will be modest relative to the market impact
that it will catalyze.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2020: S8965 died in Rules.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined. The one-time environmental product declaration tax
credit would be made eligible for two tax years to fewer than two-hun-
dred concrete and concrete component manufacturing plants operating in
New York State, and would be capped at $3,000 per plant.  If fully
subscribed, the full fiscal impact of the tax credit would not exceed
$600,000 during the two-year eligibility period. However, given that
full subscription by 100 per cent of in-state eligible firms is highly
unlikely, this figure should be considered a maximum rather than proba-
ble fiscal impact.

The low carbon concrete price discount and the supplemental CCUS price
discount defined in Section 2b and Section 3b, respectively, are
projected to result in negligible fiscal impact or no fiscal impact at
all. The price discount mechanism is designed to create an incentive for
offerers that links competitiveness for state contracts to superior GWP
performance. It is not designed to perversely encourage offerers to
escalate bid pricing, nor does it entail the direct or indirect transfer
of payments, in such forms as rebates or tax credits, to offererers as
compensation for incorporating low carbon concrete into bid proposals.
Offerers, unaware of the prices proposed by other offerers, remain high-
ly incentivized to submit bids that are as price competitive as possi-
ble. Further, market analysis supports that many high impact, market
ready carbon reduction processes and products that would increase GWP
performance and therefore bid competitiveness - including many forms of
cement substitution and carbon utilization - are not strongly associated
with premium pricing. Thus offerers are incentivized to adopt low carbon
concrete processes and products that are market ready and cost compet-
itive in order to increase their competitiveness for state contracts
vis-a-vis other offerers. This is applied for assessment and scoring
purposes only, and does not entail the transfer of any direct financial
incentive to high GWP performing bidders. All bidders remain incentiv-
ized to submit bids that maximize cost competitiveness.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S542A

SPONSOR: KAMINSKY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the state finance law, in relation to provisions in
state procurement contracts involving the use of low embodied carbon
concrete

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would establish procurement guidelines for the procurement of
low embodied carbon concrete.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill requires the Office of General Services to estab-
lish guidelines concerning the procurement of low embodied carbon
concrete. Contractors doing this type of work would then need to follow
these guidelines and certify that their work and the concrete they are
procuring meets these minimum guidelines. The bill outlines what the
office will need to examine when crafting the guidelines including
incentives for the procurement and usage of low embodied carbon concrete
by contractors. The bill requires the guidance and any associated legis-
lative recommendations to be issued to the governor and the legislature.

Section 2 of the bill is the effective date.

 
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ORIGINAL AND AMENDED VERSION:

The bill now requires the issuance of procurement guidelines by the
Office of General Services. The tax credit associated with the bill has
been removed.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

More than 10 billion tons of concrete are produced globally each year,
making it the second-most used substance on earth after water. The
production of concrete's core ingredient cement accounts for up to 8% of
total global emissions. To bring the concrete and cement sectors in line

must fall by 16% by 2030. However, current trajectories project that

Under this business as usual scenario, production escalation on this
scale will release extraordinary levels of CO2 during the next three
pivotal decades.

Therefore reducing the embodied carbon of concrete - a measure of emis-
sions generated during the production process of materials before they
are utilized - is a critical front in the collective global effort to

This bill proposes a new procurement standard for construction projects

positioned to assume given the bold commitments established by the
Climate Leadership and Community Production Act of 2019, and the size
and dynamism of the state's economy and construction industries.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2020: S8965 died in Rules.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the one hundred eightieth day after it
shall have become a law and shall apply to any state contracting oppor-
tunities advertised on or after such date and shall exclude contracts
for which an invitation for bid, request for proposal, or similar solic-
itation has been issued prior to the effective date of this act.
